overview: Two closely related Gram-negative enteric rods that both cause diarrheal disease but differ sharply in infectious dose, motility, and disease mechanism.
genZNote: Salmonella swims in, Shigella just needs a few friends to crash the party.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: A motile, Gram-negative rod causing gastroenteritis (non-typhoidal) or typhoid fever (S. Typhi), typically via contaminated food or water.
aspects.valueB: A non-motile, Gram-negative rod causing bacillary dysentery (shigellosis) via a very low infectious dose.

aspects.label: Infectious Dose
aspects.valueA: Relatively high infectious dose typically required.
aspects.valueB: Very low infectious dose (as few as 10-100 organisms) due to acid resistance.

aspects.label: Biochemical Characteristics
aspects.valueA: H2S-positive, lactose-non-fermenter, motile on TSI/motility media.

aspects.label: Virulence Mechanism
aspects.valueA: Invades intestinal epithelium via a Type III secretion system encoded on Salmonella pathogenicity islands.
aspects.valueB: Invades colonic epithelium and spreads cell-to-cell via actin-based motility; may produce Shiga toxin.

aspects.label: Clinical Relevance
aspects.valueA: Ranges from self-limited gastroenteritis to invasive typhoid/paratyphoid fever with bacteremia.
aspects.valueB: Classic cause of bloody, mucus-containing dysentery with severe abdominal cramping.

aspects.label: Identification
aspects.valueA: Grows on selective media like XLD or Hektoen enteric agar, producing black-centered (H2S+) colonies.
aspects.valueB: Grows on XLD/Hektoen agar without black centers (H2S-negative), motility-negative on stab media.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueB: Non-motile, H2S-negative, extremely low infectious dose.
